## The idea

Transcription begins before the first note. It begins with a source you can
identify, revisit, and use under terms you understand. I used to treat the
score as raw material and write down its address later. That reverses the
useful order. A source without provenance is hard to check, and an arrangement
without a licence note is hard to share.

Three libraries offer different discovery routes. IMSLP includes scans and
editions whose status can vary by item and jurisdiction. Mutopia offers typeset
scores with displayed item terms. MuseScore hosts community uploads, where
access and rights need checking piece by piece. Public domain is a legal status,
not a musical period. Its rules differ by country, and a recent engraving,
translation, or arrangement can have protection even when the underlying
composition is old. Record what the page says on the day you use it.

The working object is a small source record: title, composer, edition or
arranger, repository, page address, licence statement, access date, and the
bars you intend to transcribe. Keep that record beside the score data.

## Run this

This program turns one candidate record into an audible audition. The notes are
a tiny invented phrase, so the code does not pretend to reproduce a named
edition.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 84
use_synth :piano

candidate = {
  title: "Practice candidate",
  repository: "replace with the source collection",
  licence: "copy the exact statement from the source page",
  accessed: "YYYY-MM-DD",
  bars: "1-4",
  notes: [:c4, :d4, :e4, :g4, :e4, :d4, :c4],
  durations: [0.5, 0.5, 1, 1, 0.5, 0.5, 2]
}

candidate[:notes].zip(candidate[:durations]).each do |note_name, duration|
  play note_name, release: duration * 0.8
  sleep duration
end

puts "Source: #{candidate[:repository]}"
puts "Licence note: #{candidate[:licence]}"
```

You hear a seven-note phrase and see the incomplete source fields in the log.
The incomplete text is deliberate. It makes an undocumented candidate noisy
before you invest time in it.

## Change one thing

1. Replace the repository and licence strings with details copied from one real
   candidate page. Keep the wording exact. Listen to the phrase again, then
   check that the log gives another person enough information to find the same
   page.
2. Replace the notes and durations with the first complete phrase from a
   candidate whose terms permit your intended use. Preserve the bar range.
   Listen for a clean ending. An arbitrary four-bar cut often stops in the
   middle of a cadence.
3. Add an edition or arranger field. If the page names neither, write
   "not stated" rather than guessing. The sound does not change; the source
   record becomes more honest.

## Why it works

Programmers already separate a value from its metadata when the metadata
controls later operations. A file's bytes do not tell you whether redistribution
is permitted. Notes have the same limitation. The pitches can be identical
while the scan, engraving, or arrangement has different terms.

The source record also protects the transcription process. If bar 7 sounds
wrong next week, you know which artifact to reopen. Measure numbers mean
something only relative to an edition. If a later editor changes line breaks or
adds a pickup bar, the repository and edition fields explain the discrepancy.

Build a shortlist before choosing the capstone. Twenty candidates is enough to
expose practical differences: range, texture, score clarity, recording
availability, and licence terms. Keep the musical filter narrow. For the first
ear transcription, favour a clear monophonic line. For the score project,
favour readable engraving and stable measure numbers.

This lesson is a workflow, not legal advice. When the status is unclear, do not
invent certainty from the composer's death date alone. Choose a source with a
clear statement or obtain advice appropriate to where and how you plan to
publish.

## Take it further

Create sources.md with twenty candidates. Give each entry a stable page address,
the displayed licence or public-domain statement, access date, edition or
arranger when named, approximate difficulty, texture, and a proposed bar range.
Finish with a three-item shortlist: one melody for ear transcription, one score
for exact entry, and one larger candidate for a capstone. The structural
constraint is that another reader can recover every source without asking you
which version you meant.
